axes.question: Germany numerical fiscal-rule preferences -> coalition -> Council safeguards?
Franco-German initiative -> Commission uptake -> European Council compromise?
German withholding of support -> delayed adoption -> e-fuels accommodation while core target survives?

causal.causal_right: documented preference plus coalition plus matched negotiated outcome -> safeguards adopted
causal.counter: The outcome was negotiated by all member states and Parliament; German sources self-attribute influence.
causal.limit: Specific negotiated influence is supported; unique marginal German authorship is not isolated.
causal.mechanism: German quantitative fiscal-rule preferences -> coalition support -> Council negotiation -> debt/deficit safeguards

causal.causal_right: joint bilateral initiative -> supranational proposal uptake -> 27-state negotiated outcome
causal.counter: The final 750 billion package differed materially from the 500 billion bilateral initiative and required European Council agreement.
causal.limit: Joint agenda-setting and proposal influence supported; unilateral German control refuted.
causal.mechanism: Franco-German recovery initiative -> Commission uptake -> European Council recovery compromise

causal.causal_right: credible withholding of qualified-majority support -> delay -> negotiated concession while core rule survives
causal.counter: Germany did not remove the 2035 100 percent CO2 fleet target and the e-fuels route remained conditional on later legal implementation.
causal.limit: Procedural leverage and bounded concession supported; complete policy control not supported.
causal.mechanism: German withholding of support -> blocking minority/postponement -> e-fuels accommodation -> final adoption

causal.gap: No comparative design isolates economic weight itself from coalition, presidency, institutional rules, domestic bargaining and other member-state preferences.
causal.limit: Three cases show different institutional mechanisms and significant constraints; no cross-domain marginal-effect denominator.
causal.mechanism: German economic weight -> systematic control of EU outcomes across policy domains

claims.claim: Germany converted a specific preference for quantitative fiscal safeguards into a Council framework containing materially similar safeguards through coalition and negotiation.
claims.counter: Final text was a Council/Parliament compromise and German post-hoc attribution does not isolate unique marginal authorship.
claims.gap: Unique German marginal effect versus aligned states and presidency compromise is not separately identified.

claims.claim: Germany generally controls EU decisions because of its economic weight.
The 2020 recovery fund shows joint Franco-German agenda-setting followed by Commission uptake and a materially modified 27-state compromise, not unilateral German command.
In the 2035 car file, Germany used late procedural leverage with other states to delay adoption and obtain an e-fuels pathway while the 100 percent fleet CO2 target remained intact.
claims.counter: The final e-fuels route remained subject to later Commission proposal, EU law and climate-neutrality conditions.

claims.claim: The observed German influence mechanisms are heterogeneous and case-specific: coalition-building, bilateral agenda-setting and blocking-minority leverage cannot be collapsed into one domination mechanism.

controls.control: procedural veto leverage != complete policy victory

facts.subject: DE_FISCAL_POSITION
facts.value: Germany considered the Commission April 2023 fiscal-rule proposal insufficient and demanded clear, uniform numerical minimum requirements.

facts.subject: DE_DEBT_SAFEGUARD_PROPOSAL
facts.value: Germany proposed an independent common safeguard requiring annual debt-ratio reduction of at least 1 percentage point for high-debt states and 0.5 percentage point for medium-debt states above 60 percent.

facts.subject: FISCAL_COALITION_11
facts.value: Finance ministers from 11 of 27 EU member states jointly endorsed clear and simple expenditure rules applicable across countries.

facts.subject: COUNCIL_FISCAL_SAFEGUARDS
facts.value: The Council agreement required both a debt sustainability safeguard and a deficit resilience safeguard in the technical trajectory.

facts.subject: DE_OUTCOME_ATTRIBUTION
facts.value: The German Finance Ministry stated after adoption that the debt-sustainability and deficit-resilience safeguards originated from Germany demand for quantitative minimum requirements.

facts.subject: FR_DE_RECOVERY_INITIATIVE
facts.value: Germany and France jointly proposed a 500 billion euro European recovery fund aimed at the sectors and regions hardest hit by the pandemic.

facts.subject: COMMISSION_TAKES_FRDE_ELEMENTS
facts.value: Merkel stated that the Commission had incorporated many aspects of the Franco-German initiative into its MFF and recovery-programme proposal.

facts.subject: EUCO_RECOVERY_COMPROMISE
facts.value: The European Council final compromise authorised up to 750 billion euro of EU borrowing for Next Generation EU, combining loans and expenditure rather than reproducing the Franco-German proposal unchanged.

facts.subject: DE_EFUELS_POSITION
facts.value: German transport minister Volker Wissing publicly insisted that the Commission deliver a route for registering new combustion-engine vehicles after 2035 when operated with synthetic fuels.

facts.subject: DE_EFUELS_BLOCKING_EFFECT
facts.value: Germany last-minute refusal to support the already-negotiated 2035 car measure contributed to postponement of the formal approval vote and, with other states, created a blocking minority.

facts.subject: FINAL_CARS_2035
facts.value: The Council ultimately adopted the 100 percent CO2 reduction target for new cars and vans from 2035.

facts.subject: FINAL_EFUELS_REFERENCE
facts.value: The adopted framework included a reference under which the Commission would propose a route for registering vehicles running exclusively on CO2-neutral fuels after 2035, outside fleet standards and subject to EU law and climate-neutrality objectives.

DIALECTICAL_MAP.antithesis: EU institutions, coalitions and qualified-majority rules constrain Germany and produce collective compromises.
DIALECTICAL_MAP.synthesis: German influence is materially observable but mechanism-specific: coalition-building, joint agenda-setting and blocking-minority leverage. These channels can produce identifiable deltas without establishing general German control of the EU.
DIALECTICAL_MAP.thesis: Germany can convert national preferences into EU outcomes through superior structural power.
